profiles.name: Benjamin Kontrowitz
profiles.description:
Benjamin Kontrowitz was born 1882 in Ekaterinoslav, Russia (present-day Dnipro, Ukraine). Worked as a silk weaver. Immigrated to the United States in 1916.

A former member of the Left Wing of the Socialist Party of America and joined the Russian Federation of the Communist Party of America in 1919. He served as recording secretary, an executive board member, and a lecturer for its Paterson, New Jersey branch, and was a delegate to the First Convention of the Jewish Communist Federation in October 1919. Also a member of the IWW’s Textile Workers’ Industrial Union. Arrested during the second Palmer Raids in January 1920, he was deported on November 23, 1920. He was married and had a son living in Paterson.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Christopher Hetaguroff
profiles.description:
Christopher Hetaguroff was employed as a laborer.

Joined the Society for the Relief of Russia, then in 1919 joined the Communist Party in Seattle and was elected secretary of his branch. Arrested in January 1920, and immigration authorities issued a deportation warrant describing him as both an anarchist and “likely to become a public charge,” arguing that this charge was “borne out by the fact that thru his radical activities and membership he is now a public charge in the jail at Seattle, Wash.” Hetaguroff protested the designation, stating, “I would not become a public charge; I can work.” Deported aboard the SS Stockholm on January 22, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Feodor Korini
profiles.description:
Feodor Korini was born about 1888 in Chernihiv, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Served as financial secretary of Russian Branch No. 2 of the Communist Party in Philadelphia under the pseudonym “Butzki.” Arrested in January 1920, he denied the identity, but multiple witnesses identified him as such. An immigration inspector characterized his testimony as “shifting, evasive, and evidently untruthful in material particulars.” He was deported to Russia on February 26, 1921.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.name: Julius Manninger
profiles.description:
Julius Manninger was born 1896 in Ponitz, Austria-Hungary (present-day Hungary). Immigrated to the United States in 1909.

Joined the Socialist Party and attended a single meeting of the Communist Party of America. Arrested January 1920 in Fort Wayne, Indiana, he was deported to Austria June 22, 1920 as an alleged Communist Party member.

In February 1921 Assistant Secretary of Labor Louis F. Post concluded that the deportation had been carried out in error due to a misunderstanding of the facts. Manninger returned to the United States in December 1921 under his family name, Pichler, and declared his intention to become a US citizen.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.description:
Nick Federov was born 1884 in Samara, Russia. Immigrated to the United States in 1907.

profiles.name: Platon Prokuda
profiles.description:
Platon Prokuda was born 1893 in Russia. Immigrated to the United States in 1912.

Joined the Socialist Party and later the Union of Russian Workers in Detroit. After authorities broke up the URW in November 1919 he attended Communist Party events but did not join, stating he remained an anarchist “Because no matter what government it is, there is always scandal there, fraud, graft, and all that sort of stuff.” Arrested January 1920 and held at Fort Wayne. Deported to Russia February 26, 1921.

Refused entry at Libau with several other deportees because of his anarchism. Co-authored “An Open Letter to the Russian Premier Vladimir Lenin” in response. Last known to be stranded in Danzig.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.
